A good idea, in theory, but Chess is inevitably a war of attrition. It's about achieving your goals on the battlefield by causing as much damage to your opponent as you can whilst preventing him from doing the same to you, while you drive him into a corner. That may have worked for medieval times, but today we live in a very tightly populated world that magnifies the effects of attrition exponentially, as a result.

If you want a "Thinking Man's Wargame", then get them started playing Go. The rules are much simpler than learning all of the rules of chess (including the variant moves such as en passant and castling) making it much easier to get started at an earlier age, the skill to master requires much more focus and aptitude, allowing for much more levels of mastery. Further, the game is one, first and foremost, of territory and resources. This is the very thing wars are fought over to begin with, and it's something the West seems to have forgotten, with their focus as it has been on Attrition Wars instead of wars that capture Territory.

Your opponent cannot fight you if his troops have no territory to garrison on, no resources to run his war machine, and no capitol to issue his commands from. Go emphasizes this reality of warfare, and thus Territory, and the gain of it, as a game mechanic becomes the primary objective to winning. In an age where the Enemy can retain Territory that is technically within your borders (Think: ISIS taking over a town in Iraq, a nation within territory we "control", so to speak, or at the very least allied with us), this reality, and knowing how to counter it so as to regain said Territory for your own use, without eradicating that land's usefulness through attrition, become paramount.
